backTranslations.41:
**Before the appointment**
- Add the appointment date in the Appointment tab. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are and what would make them more complete.
- Pick the topics and questions that matter most. Keep them to three or four.
- Create your notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**At the appointment**
- Give or show the first page. It is designed to be read in under a minute: numbers, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and are not**

They are a summary of what you logged, together with whatever you chose to bring from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis nor a complete medical record, and any patterns they contain are coincidence checks, not proof of cause. Your doctor may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the appointment**

Add any new medication with its start date. In a few weeks, MenoMap can show you your entries before and after, which makes the next follow-up easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a specific point in time: the day on which 12 consecutive months without a period are completed, when this is not explained by something else (such as pregnancy, certain medications or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early 50s, but it is common for it to happen at any time from the mid-40s to the mid-50s.

**Perimenopause** is the years leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods may become irregular, heavier, lighter, closer together or further apart. Many of the changes associated with menopause, such as hot flushes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often start in this phase, while there is still a period. Perimenopause can last a few years or considerably more, and it shows up differently in each person.

**Postmenopause** is the whole time after that 12-month boundary. Some symptoms fade over time, while others may continue for years.

Menopause can also come earlier because of surgery that removes the ovaries, certain cancer treatments or other conditions. Menopause before 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth discussing with a doctor.

**How it is recognized.** In many people over 45, doctors recognize perimenopause or menopause from your history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed, because hormone levels change from day to day. They are more likely to be done when someone is younger or the picture is not clear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do is keep an honest record of what you notice: waves, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor see the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flushes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flush is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with redness, sweating, a fast heartbeat or chills afterwards. A night sweat is the same thing during sleep and can be so intense that it wakes you or soaks your sheets.

They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people have few and mild ones, others have many a day, which disrupt work and sleep. In some people they fade within a few years, in others they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** Patterns are often noticed with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress or heavy covers. These differ a lot from person to person, so tracking your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes too.** Flushing and sweating can also be due to thyroid problems, infections, certain medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern or come with weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, mention it to a doctor.

**How to describe them well.** Useful details for an appointment:
- How many per day and how many at night, roughly
- How intense you feel them and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to come before
- What you have tried and whether anything changed

MenoMap's 'Wave' button and logging after the fact exist precisely so you can record these without much effort.

**Help exists.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, as well as practical approaches. Which ones suit you is something to discuss with a doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often referred to as hormone replacement therapy, HRT) replaces part of the estrogen that the body produces in smaller amounts around menopause. Major guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats for many people, and it may help with other symptoms too.

**It comes in several forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets and low-dose vaginal preparations for local symptoms such as dryness. In people who still have a uterus, a progestogen is usually prescribed together with the estrogen, to protect the inner lining of the uterus.

**The benefits and risks depend on the person:** age, how much time has passed since the periods stopped, personal and family history (for example of breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease) and the type and way the treatment is given. That is why it is a decision you make together with a doctor who knows your history, not something an app can decide.

**Questions that are commonly asked:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- Which type and which form would you recommend to me, and why?
- What benefits could I expect and how soon?
- What are my own risks and how do they compare with not having treatment?
- What should I watch for and when should we review it?

**If you are already taking it,** log it in MenoMap (You → Medications). MenoMap will show your waves before and after starting, as a coincidence check and not as proof, so you have something concrete to discuss at the review.

MenoMap never recommends starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not suitable for everyone, and some people simply prefer other paths. There are several.

**Prescription options.** Certain non-hormonal medications have evidence that they reduce hot flushes. These include certain medications originally developed for other conditions, as well as a newer class designed specifically for hot flushes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talking therapies and mind-body approaches.** Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause has evidence that it makes hot flushes and night sweats less bothersome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes that many people find useful:**
- Layered clothing that you take off quickly
- A fan at the desk and next to the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable covers
- Noticing and limiting your personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help with this)
- Regular physical activity and a steady sleep schedule

**Supplements and herbal products.** The evidence for many of them is mixed or limited, quality varies and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about anything you take, even over-the-counter products.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own entries before and during a change, which is easier to judge than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short, and it is hard to remember a whole month of nights on the spot. We usually remember the most recent or the worst days. A simple log covers that gap.

**What a diary gives your doctor:**
- How often symptoms appear and how intense they are, not just that they appear
- Whether things are improving, getting worse or staying the same
- What was happening around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A reference point for comparison, if you try a treatment

**Keep it simple.** A diary only helps if you keep it up. MenoMap is built around a one-tap 'Wave' button and an evening check-in of four questions, so it takes seconds, not a whole notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of entries usually show a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Appointment tab helps you pick questions and prints them together with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
Once 12 months have passed without a period, **any vaginal bleeding should be checked by a doctor**, even if it happened only once, and even if it was only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge.

Most of the time the cause turns out not to be serious. Thinning of the vaginal wall or of the inner lining of the uterus, for example, is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much more easily treated when found early. That is why public health guidance says to get it checked and not to wait.

**If you are on hormone therapy,** some bleeding patterns may be expected, depending on the type you take. Bleeding that is not expected for your treatment, is heavier than usual or happens at the wrong time must also be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or your health service and say that you had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, the amount and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can keep this for you (You → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding happened. It will remind you that it should be checked and will include it in your appointment notes.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is among the most common complaints in midlife and rarely has a single cause.

**Night sweats** may wake you immediately or leave you so hot or damp that you cannot fall back asleep.

**Other common factors:**
- Needing to urinate at night
- Anxiety or a racing mind
- Alcohol, which may help you fall asleep but usually makes sleep broken in the second half of the night
- Caffeine late in the day
- Pain, restless legs or the snoring of the person next to you
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which may be a sign of sleep apnea (worth mentioning, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What usually helps.** A cool, dark room, breathable covers and layered clothing that you take off easily, a steady wake-up time and less alcohol close to bedtime. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied approach, and many doctors can direct you to it.

**What to log.** For a week or two, note your sleep rating, night waves, alcohol and caffeine late in the day. MenoMap's evening check-in and wave logging do this in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside your night sweats, as context and not as an explanation.

**When to get it checked.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example when driving), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice pauses in your breathing or that you gasp for air at night.
